explanation: The Yamuna joins the Ganges far downstream. Inside, the emperor's cenotaph sits beside his wife's, the one break in the tomb's perfect symmetry.

claims.text: The Taj Mahal stands on the southern bank of the Yamuna river in Agra.
The Taj Mahal does not stand on the Ganges, the Indus or the Brahmaputra.
The Yamuna flows into the Ganges downstream of Agra, at Prayagraj.
The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
The emperor's cenotaph, placed beside his wife's, is the one element that breaks the symmetry of the Taj Mahal's design.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: The caveat is that "only asymmetry" is an overstatement. A 2016 study in Current Science, reported by Open magazine, found the central dome itself is asymmetrical. ... So the cenotaph is the most-cited deviation, but not the sole one.

claimResults.note: Not confirmed as written. Many sources call Shah Jahan's cenotaph the one break in symmetry, but a peer-reviewed study reported by Open magazine finds the central dome asymmetrical too, so 'the one element' is an overstatement.

issues.note: c5: 'the one break in the tomb's perfect symmetry' is an 'only' claim over a fixed set, and a 2016 Current Science study (reported by Open magazine) found the central dome asymmetrical as well. The cenotaph is the best-known deviation, not the only one. Reword to 'a famous break in the tomb's symmetry'. The key (Yamuna) is sound.
